title: How To Get Your Students To Show Up For Online Learning nline-learning/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Written just weeks into pandemic school closures, this unusually candid piece criticizes school and district leadership for dumping unclear online-learning mandates on stressed teachers without adequate guidance. Linsin argues that teachers cannot force attendance through threats or consequences when families are dealing with far more urgent concerns like health, food, and finances, and calls for more compassion all around. His practical recommendation is to shift toward project-based learning with a once-a-day check-in, giving students engaging, creative long-term projects rather than trying to replicate a full classroom schedule online. He specifically champions read-aloud sessions as a way to build connection and comfort. He acknowledges some parents will complain no matter what, and counsels teachers to extend grace and move on rather than trying to please everyone.
points: Criticizes district and school leadership for rolling out untested online-learning mandates without clear guidance for teachers.
Argues that threats and consequences cannot compel attendance when families face more urgent concerns like health and finances.
Recommends centering online instruction on engaging, creative project-based learning with a once-a-day check-in rather than replicating a full school day.
Champions read-aloud sessions as a simple, high-value way to build connection and ease students' fears during remote learning.
Advises teachers to accept that they cannot please every parent and to extend themselves grace under impossible circumstances.
quotes: Shame on the school districts and administrators that enabled this to happen. Shame on them for rolling out programs and floating ideas that haven’t been tested.
Moreover, there are way more important things on the minds of many of our students and families. Like health, food, and finances.
I suggest a focus on project-based learning, with a once-a-day check in. Go ahead and provide online links to resources if students want to do more.
You can’t please everyone. And if they don’t understand the pickle you’re in, or grasp this most unusual moment in history, or the confusion at the district and administrative levels, then so be it.
Use the online video platform of your choice as an opportunity to read great books, regardless of what you teach or how old your students.
Use your daily connection with your students to ease their fears. To get back to basics.
